response.text:
Of what they had to expect, the Minister knew no more than his son. What he or Mr. Seward or Mr. Sumner may have thought is the affair of history and their errors concern historians. The errors of a private secretary concerned no one but himself, and were a large part of his education. He sailed on May 12 supposing he was going to a friendly Government and people, true to anti-slavery principles which had been their steadiest profession. For a hundred years the chief effort of his family had aimed at bringing the Government of England into intelligent coöperation with the objects and interests of America. His father was about to make a new effort; the chance of success seemed promising; the slave States had been the chief apparent obstacle to good understanding. As for the private secretary himself, he was, like all Bostonians, instinctively English. He could not conceive the idea of a hostile England. As one of a famous anti-slavery family, he supposed himself welcome everywhere in the British Islands.

On May 13, he met the official announcement that England recognized the belligerency of the Confederacy. This beginning of a new education tore up by the roots nearly all that was left of Harvard College and Germany. He had to learn—soonest best—that his ideas were the reverse of truth; that in May, 1861, no one in England—literally no one—doubted that Jefferson Davis had made or would make a nation, and nearly all were glad of it, though not often saying so. Lord John Russell, as Foreign Secretary, had received the rebel emissaries and decided to recognize their belligerency before Mr. Adams’s arrival, in order to fix the British position in advance; recognition of independence would then be a matter of time and occasion.

Whatever the Minister may have felt, the first effect on his son was a dullness of comprehension, a hazy inability to grasp the missile or realize the blow. Yet he realized that to his father it was likely to be fatal, and that the family might turn round and go home in a few weeks. He came, long afterwards, to grow cold at the thought of his situation had his father shown himself what Sumner thought him—unfit for his post. That the private secretary was unfit for his—trifling though it were—was proved by his unreflecting confidence in his father. It never entered his mind that his father might lose his nerve or temper; he passed this long day and tedious journey to London without once thinking his father might make a mistake. Whatever the Minister thought—and his thought was not less active than his son’s—he showed no trace of excitement; mind and temper perfectly balanced; not a word escaped; not a nerve twitched.

The test was final, for no other shock so violent and sudden could possibly recur. The worst was in full sight. For once the private secretary knew his own business, which was to imitate his father as closely as possible and hold his tongue. Dumped into a hotel at the foot of Regent Street in the midst of a London season, without a friend or even an acquaintance, he preferred to laugh at the Minister’s bewilderment before the waiter’s “’amhandheggsir” rather than ask a question or express a doubt. If taken seriously, the situation was appalling to face; had he known it better, he would only have thought it worse.

Socially, under the best of circumstances, a newcomer in London needs years; the Minister had not a week or an hour to spare; the son had no chance of beginning. Politically the prospect looked worse for Seward and Sumner than for the Minister on the spot, for Mr. Adams was one of the luckiest of men in what he achieved and in what he escaped. Lord John Russell had acted—had meant to act—kindly in forestalling his arrival. The blow must have fallen within three months and would then have broken him down. British Ministers were a little ashamed of themselves and certain to wait the longer for their next step in proportion to the haste of their first.

This is not the story of Charles Francis Adams’s diplomatic adventures, but of his son’s search for an education, which, if not taken too seriously, tended to humor. The father’s position in London was not altogether bad; the son’s was absurd. Thanks to certain family associations, the elder Adams naturally looked on British Ministers as enemies—Downing Street had been the hereditary foe of the Adamses—but the Government, even when officially rude, liked to be personally civil; a diplomatic agent is none the worse for being put in a corner. The son had no such compensations. Brought over to help his father, he could conceive no way of helping him; he was clear that his father had got to help him. To him, the Legation was social ostracism, terrible beyond anything he had known. Entire solitude in the great society of London was doubly desperate because his duties required him to know everybody and to go everywhere his parents needed escort. He had no friend, or even enemy, to tell him to be patient; had any one done it, he would have broken out that patience was the last resource of fools as well as of sages.

He soon doubted whether secretaries were meant to be useful. Wars were too common in diplomacy to disturb the diplomat’s habits. At a club to which the Minister’s son could go only as a guest, the most instructive conversation he ever heard among young men of his own age who hung about the tables, more helpless than himself, was, “Quel chien de pays!” No one wanted to discuss affairs; that was their chiefs’ business, and chiefs were slow to assume work not ordered from their Courts. Empires were always tumbling to pieces and diplomats always picking them up.

His social education was barer still and more trying to vanity. His mistakes in etiquette made him writhe. He never forgot an afternoon when he hid himself in a window embrasure, or a garden-party where he watched a great house empty and the young lord and cousins set to playing leap-frog on the lawn, or a dance where an alarming hostess seized him and forced him into a Highland fling before the assembled nobility and gentry, with an ambassador’s daughter for partner. To him the world turned to ashes.

When the end of the season came, he had not won a private acquaintance, and he hugged solitude when the story of Bull Run appeared. Bull Run was a worse diplomatic than military disaster, yet the Legation, to its surprise, found the effect almost strengthening. They no longer felt doubt. For the next year they went from week to week, ready to leave England at once and never assuming more than three months as their limit. Europe waited to see them go; so certain was the end that no one cared to hurry it.

He looked on himself as about to begin a final education in the ranks of the Army of the Potomac, where most of his friends were enjoying a pleasanter life than his own. With this idea he passed summer and autumn and began the winter. Any winter in London is a severe trial; one’s first winter is the most trying; but December, 1861, in a black fog would have gorged a glutton of gloom.

One afternoon, struggling against nervous depression in the solitude of Mansfield Street during the Minister’s absence on a country visit, Reuter’s telegram announcing the seizure of Mason and Slidell from a British mail-steamer was brought to the office. All three secretaries, public and private, were there, nervous as wild beasts under long strain, and all three—though they knew it to be not merely departure-orders, not merely diplomatic rupture, but a declaration of war—broke into shouts of delight. They were glad to face the end. They saw it and cheered it! Since England was waiting only for its own moment to strike, they were eager to strike first. They telegraphed the news to the Minister. The moment was for him the crisis of his career; for the secretaries it was merely the beginning of another intolerable delay. At the sharpest suspense, the Prince Consort sickened and died. Portland Place at Christmas was never rosy, but in 1861 the most hardened Londoner lost his ruddiness. The private secretary had one comfort—they should not be private secretaries long.

He was mistaken—of course! He had been mistaken at every point of his education, and kept up the same mistake for nearly seven years, deluded by the notion that the end was near. To him the Trent Affair was only one of many affairs to be copied in a delicate round hand into his books, but it had results personal to him. One was to end forever the idea of being “useful.” As an independent citizen, not in Government employ, he had kept up relations with the American press, written to New York, talked with friendly London newspapers, tried to give them news and views that should not clash. He even went to Manchester to study the cotton famine and wrote a long account which was printed with his name, and instantly came back on him in crushing shape—a satirical leader in the Times. He learned the narrowness of his escape from exposure; he also learned the value of obscurity. No one thought twice about the article; the world had other favorite objects of ridicule. He escaped, but never tried to be useful again. The Trent Affair dwarfed individual effort. His education reached the point of seeing its own proportions. “Surtout point de zèle!” Zeal was too hazardous a profession for a Minister’s son to pursue among Trent Affairs and rebel cruisers. He wrote no more letters and meddled with no more newspapers, though he felt unkindly towards the editor of the Times. The storm passed like a snow-squall, leaving the Legation still in place. He sat down again to copy papers, file letters, and read London judgments on the incapacity of Mr. Lincoln and the brutality of Mr. Seward—or vice versa.

The months dragged. He had one social relief, a house on the Thames where a charming woman made a refuge that was a liberal education, a single source of warmth and light during two years of solitude. Otherwise the Legation was home, and all inmates made common cause; one lived, but was merely flayed alive. Yet, while this was true of the younger members, it was not quite so with the Minister and Mrs. Adams. Very slowly, they gained foothold. British society began with violent prejudice against Lincoln, Seward, and all Republicans except Sumner; the private secretary suspected Americans in New York and Boston had something to do with it; the Copperhead was at home in Pall Mall; the average Englishman liked coarseness and would have liked Lincoln and Seward the better had they been ruffians. The Minister’s quiet manner and unassailable position in no way conciliated them; they chose to ignore him since they could not ridicule him. Lord John Russell set the example; personally the Minister was kindly treated; politically negligible; there to be put aside. Every one waited to see Washington crumble and the Minister vanish.

This made him an exception among diplomats. Europe fought and treated within a family, rarely in view of total extinction; but for a year at least Europe regarded the Washington Government as dead and its Ministers as nullities. Mr. Adams was better received than most nullities because he made no noise. Little by little, society took the habit of accepting him, not as a diplomat, but as a member of opposition, an eminent counsel retained for a foreign Government. Barriers of race, language, habit, ceased to exist; Earl Russell could not hold him apart; he was undistinguishable from a Londoner; few Londoners were so widely at home; none had such double personality and double weight.

A singular luck never deserted him. Friends who needed support, and were relieved to find it, proclaimed to all the world their estimate of his character, and between them he was almost safe. The private secretary saw the ring begin to clear for heavy-weights to stand up in a prize-fight likely to be brutal enough, and the Ministry, after the Trent Affair, felt a little ashamed and disposed to wait. Little by little, friends gathered who were no fair-weather companions—parliamentary allies and social houses that gave the Legation weight. He even found himself one night, after dinner, engaged in instructing John Stuart Mill on the peculiar merits of an American protective system, and insisted, afterwards, that it was not the claret that led him into loquacity, but Mr. Mill’s assenting politeness.

Friendliness he found here and there, chiefly among elders; not among fashionable or socially powerful people, although not even this rule was strict. A few houses grew almost familiar; a few radical young men were cordial. By the time society began to reopen its doors after the Prince Consort’s death, he occasionally saw a face he knew, although he made no more effort of any kind, but silently waited the end. Whatever the advantages of social relations to his father and mother, to him the whole business of diplomacy and society was futile. He meant to go home.
